study.brief_markdown:
## Question
In Houston, do apartment communities with more green cover have higher asking rents?

## Answer
No; green cover percentage is not significantly associated with asking rents among Houston apartment buildings.

## Method
The analysis sampled 40 [E1] apartment buildings from Houston's CoStar database. All 40 [E1] buildings were inspected using satellite imagery to measure green cover percentage, which ranged from 2% [E40] to 55% [E85, E118]. Green cover was defined by vision inspection of a small square around each address point. A linear regression with robust standard errors was performed to estimate the relationship between green cover percentage (predictor) and maximum asking rent (outcome), controlling for building size, year built, number of units, and building class [E122].

## Result
Each additional percentage point of green cover is associated with $0.077 [E122] lower asking rent (95% CI [$26.8, $26.7], p = 0.996 [E122]), controlling for building characteristics. This association is not statistically significant. The sample size was n = 40 [E122] buildings.

## Confidence and caveats
This study has several important limitations. First, this is an observational association only and does not show cause and effect. Second, correlation is not causation; many unmeasured factors—including neighborhood prestige, proximity to employment, and amenity quality—likely influence both green cover and rents. Third, the confidence interval is very wide, indicating substantial uncertainty in the estimate. Fourth, image measurements cover a small square around each address point, which may not represent the full extent of the apartment community. Fifth, the study uses real data from Houston, so results may not generalize to other markets.
caveats: Observational association only; this does not show cause and effect.
Image measurements cover the Vexcel parcel or 80 m square, which may not match the whole community.
